analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $10.10 an hour and indexes it to inflation.
analysis.headline: The Fair Minimum Wage Act of 2013, raising the federal minimum wage to $10.10 an hour with a path to $12, gathered 197 Democratic cosponsors but never received a vote in the House.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would raise the federal minimum wage from $7.25 in stages, first to $9.80, then to $10.10, then to $12 over six years, and adjust it annually with inflation. It would also gradually raise the tipped minimum wage to 70% of the full minimum wage. It never received a vote in the House or Senate before the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Roughly 30 million workers earning low wages would gain higher pay under this bill, including many who earn slightly above the minimum and would benefit from a higher wage floor.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage in stages from $7.25 to $9.80, then $10.10, then $12 over six years.
Raises the tipped minimum wage, currently $2.13, to $3.00 immediately and then gradually to 70% of the full minimum wage.
Indexes the minimum wage to inflation after it reaches $12, so it no longer erodes over time.

analysis.who_pays: Businesses employing low-wage workers, particularly in labor-intensive sectors like restaurants, agriculture, and retail, would face higher labor costs.

drawbacks.text: Critics argue sharply higher minimum wages reduce employment opportunities for the least experienced and least skilled workers.
Small businesses and franchise operators say rising labor costs without equivalent revenue gains force cuts in hours or jobs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Raising the minimum wage meaningfully increases pay for low-wage workers, though some research suggests trade-offs for the least experienced workers; the bill's failure left the federal minimum at $7.25 until the 118th Congress.

outcome.mechanism: The bill gathered 197 Democratic cosponsors but never received a vote in the House or Senate, and died when the 113th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. George Miller (D-CA) introduced the bill on March 6, 2013, with 197 Democratic cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce and then to its Workforce Protections Subcommittee, which did not act.

On February 26, 2014, Rep. Bishop (NY) filed a motion to discharge the committee, a maneuver to force the bill onto the floor without a committee vote; the petition did not reach the required 218 signatures.
A companion bill in the Senate, S. 460, also never received a vote; the chamber voted on a lower alternative in 2014, which fell short of the 60 votes needed.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers of minimum-wage workers are better off because the bill died; the federal minimum wage remained $7.25, leaving their labor costs unchanged for another decade.

for.name: Rep. George Miller
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited the House Democratic Caucus's support.

for.name: 197 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, representing roughly 93% of the House Democratic Caucus.

for.name: Rep. Timothy Bishop (NY)
for.what_they_did: Filed a discharge petition on February 26, 2014, to force the bill out of committee and onto the floor.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup or a floor vote during the entire Congress.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee and took no further action on it.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Opposed the Senate companion bill and blocked it from reaching the 60-vote threshold in 2014.

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely Democratic: all 197 cosponsors were Democrats, while Republican House leadership blocked the bill from any vote. In the Senate, the companion bill fell short of the 60-vote threshold along party lines.

industries.note: Restaurants employ the most minimum-wage workers and would bear the largest labor cost increases, especially for tipped workers whose base wage would rise sharply. Their interest in keeping the wage low runs against workers' interest in higher pay.
Retailers with large low-wage workforces would face higher labor costs. Like restaurants, their cost interest runs against workers' wage interests.
Small employers argue higher wage floors raise costs faster than their revenue grows, forcing cuts to hours or staffing.
